Where it ended up, not how far it went

Picture a cart on a straight track. To describe where it is, pick a zero point on the track and a positive direction, say to the right. The cart's position is then a single signed number in meters. When the cart moves, its position changes. That change is its displacement, written Δx, and it is always the final position minus the starting position.

Displacement is not the same as the distance the cart traveled. If the cart rolls 2.0 m to the right and then 2.0 m back, it traveled 4.0 m, but its displacement is zero because it ended where it began. Distance is a size only; displacement has a size and a direction, and on a line the direction is carried by the sign.

We model the cart as an object model: a single point that has a position but no size, shape or inner parts. That is enough to describe where it is and how it moves, and it keeps the arithmetic simple.

Average velocity

How quickly the position changes is the velocity. Over a time interval Δt, the cart's average velocity is its displacement divided by that interval: v = Δx/Δt. The unit is meters per second, m/s. A positive velocity means the cart moves in the positive direction; a negative one means it moves the other way.

Speed is the size of the velocity. A cart moving left at 0.5 m/s has a velocity of −0.5 m/s and a speed of 0.5 m/s. Average speed over a trip is distance over time, which can differ from the size of the average velocity when the cart turns around.

Worked example. A cart is at 0.20 m at time 0 and at 1.40 m at 3.0 s. What is its average velocity?

Δx = 1.40 m − 0.20 m = 1.20 m. Δt = 3.0 s − 0 s = 3.0 s.

v = Δx/Δt = 1.20 m / 3.0 s = 0.40 m/s, to two significant figures, in the positive direction.

Average acceleration

When the velocity itself changes, the cart is accelerating. Its average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval: a = Δv/Δt, in meters per second per second, m/s². An object accelerates whenever its speed changes or its direction of motion changes.

The sign of the acceleration compares with the sign of the velocity. If they match, the object speeds up; if they are opposite, it slows down. A car moving forward and braking has a negative acceleration, even though it is still moving forward.

Worked example. A cart's velocity rises from 0.20 m/s to 0.80 m/s in 3.0 s. What is its average acceleration?

Δv = 0.80 m/s − 0.20 m/s = 0.60 m/s.

a = Δv/Δt = 0.60 m/s / 3.0 s = 0.20 m/s².

Shorter and shorter intervals

An average describes a whole interval. When the interval is made very short, the average velocity gets closer and closer to the velocity at one instant, the instantaneous velocity, and the same is true for acceleration. A speedometer shows instantaneous speed; a trip computer shows an average.

Common slips

Three mistakes cost the most points. First, using the final position instead of the change in position: always subtract where the object started. Second, dropping the sign: slowing down while moving forward is a negative acceleration. Third, mixing centimeters and meters: convert to meters before you divide, so the answer comes out in m/s.
